feedback: If a child reads a tall stack as a long object, slide the real ruler under the plot and ask them to point to where an object of that length would actually sit; hold the two questions apart — 'how many objects?' versus 'how long is one?'

If a child treats each X as a unit of length (e.g. 'three Xs means 3 cm long'), clarify that each X stands for one object placed at its measured position; the length is read from the horizontal scale, not from how many Xs are stacked.

If a child leaves out a value nothing measured (e.g. axis reads 3,4,6,7 with 5 missing), reteach the axis as a ruler — every unit is present whether or not data lands on it; overlay a real ruler and mark the empty value together.

If a child reorders or evenly spaces only the values that occurred (as in a category chart), remind them the axis is an ordered measurement scale where position means length, so every unit must appear in order.
If every measurement is off by one unit, pause the plotting and reteach measuring from zero with gap-free unit iteration before returning.

When a child notices a whole-number value on the scale with no X above it, confirm that the empty spot is meaningful: it shows no object had that length, and the scale keeps it open. If a child has put an X at a value nothing measured, have them check their recorded data and remove it.
If a second object also measures 6, confirm its X stacks above the first at the same position — the stack grows upward (count) while the position stays fixed (length).
activities.intendedInsight: On a line plot the sideways position of an X answers 'how long?' while the upward height of a stack answers 'how many?'. Unlike reorderable categorical charts, the axis is a ruler-like measurement scale: equal intervals with every whole-number value staying on it even when no object landed there, so the gaps stay equal.
learnerActions: Collect 6-8 small real objects (pencils, crayons, leaves, blocks) and measure each to the nearest whole centimetre, measuring from the ruler's zero mark, not from 1 or the end.
Record each measurement in a simple tally or frequency table as a bridge from raw measurements to the plot.

Notice how a line plot differs from earlier tally or category charts: here the horizontal axis is an ordered measurement scale with equal whole-number intervals and every value present, not a set of arbitrary categories you could reorder or leave out.

On a horizontal line, mark the scale as equal whole-number intervals across the full range of your data, including any whole-number value that nothing measured. Early on a line that is already pre-scaled can be provided as a scaffold so you focus on plotting; building the scale yourself afterwards is the fuller skill this topic is aiming at.
Place exactly one X above each object's measured value; when two objects share a length, stack a second X on top of the first.

If your scale marks are spaced 1 cm apart, keep an actual ruler aligned directly beneath the line, with its numbers matching your scale labels, so each X's horizontal position reads as a length on the same scale.
Answer two separate questions from your finished plot: 'How many objects were 6 cm?' (count the Xs in that stack) and 'How long is the longest object?' (read its position on the scale).
activities.title: Measure your own objects, then build the line plot

feedback: If a child answers 'how long is the longest?' with a stack's count, redirect them to the horizontal scale and ask them to read the position of the rightmost X.
If a child ignores an empty scale value, ask what it tells them about objects of that length.
Confirm that adding an object changes the count of a stack but not the positions already on the plot.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a line plot means deliberately choosing between counting (height) and reading position (length); the same plot answers both kinds of question in different ways.
learnerActions: Study a completed line plot and answer count questions such as 'How many objects were 6 cm long?' by counting the Xs in a stack.
Answer position questions such as 'How long is the longest object?' by reading the scale, not the stack height.
Explain what an empty whole-number value on the scale means (no object had that length).
Predict what changes if one more object measuring 6 cm were added (one more X on the 6 stack; the position is unchanged).
activities.title: Interpret a given line plot: how many versus how long
